One one of my trips home the Comptroller of
Pan American asked why a company which sold its services only for cash
should have as by then we did three million dollars in "bills receivable".
When I told him the reason he hit the roof and we finally had to go to
President Trippe for a decision.
When the latter understood the situation
he had a good laugh and said "Bix - you win in a walk."
You will hear it
said that no company ever opperated in China without paying squeeze to
Chinese officials but we did.
The nearest we ever came to paying squeeze
was when I reluctantly agreed to the purchase of a white jade bowl which
was stolen from the Peiping treasures for presentation to an official
who was retiring as President of the compant. He had purchased the bowl
and had inscribed on a little plate on the stand " to (his name) from
C.N.A.C. Your service to this company was like the quality of this jade".
It was true that his services were about as disreputable as the acquisi-
tion of that bowl.
He was the one who was describing a tiger hunt he had
been on down in Indo China. It was at a dinner party given by the Minister
of Communications. Our hero said that he was stationed in a small tree
with the bait - a lamb - tied to a stake below him. The tiger walked all
around the tree before our Chinese friend could get a bead on him. I said
"K.C. if you had fallen out of that tree I'd bet on you and give the tiger
the first bite."
The Minister nearly died laughing and after that this
particular Chinese was always called "Tiger".
Speaking of "squeeze" one of our pilots left
the company and got a job
as the representative of an aviation company intent on selling aircraft
to the Chinese Government. Not meeing with any success our ex-pilot
approached the American Commercial Attache in Shanghai and said rather
bluntly "I want to know how you pay squeeze." The Attache said "that's
sort of asking how you make a girl - some you just say 'how's about it'
while with others you have to use a little more finesse."

. Back in 1928 the then great powers were manoeuvering for position in
the, Chinese aviation market - military and commercial. The British
Through commercial Imperial Airwayd and military Far East Aviation.
The French were using their sphere of influence in Yunnan-fu later
called Kunming which they had joined to Hanoi in French Indo China
by a railroad to promote French aviation. They had flown a number of
French planes out to Indo China and then on to Chungking where the
warlord of that province liu Hsiang (sp?) was unable to secure an im-
port permit to bring in airplanes, parts, gasoline or oil.
The so-
called Central Government which controlled Shanghai would not issue
its Huchow or import permit for any of the interior warlords but re-
served such to itself.
The Germans had formed a company called Eur-
asia which was owned two thirds by the Chinese Central Government and
the German Luft Hansa one third for the purpose of establishing air-
transport lines in China. C.M.Keyes, President of Curtiss Aeroplane
formed a group to throw the American hat in the ring. He promoted
the Aviation Exploration Co. and organized an expedition to China
under the leadership of our old friend wa. B. Robertson of St. Louis.
It was a bizarre collection of misfits.
A lawyer who knew nothing
whatever about Chinese Company law, while Shanghai had many able
American lawyers who did. An interpreter who spoke only Cantonese
to deal with officials who spoke only the northern dialect and could
not understand a word he said in Chinese but most of them spoke good
English so it didn't matter. A pilot with a Loening Amphibian. They
negotiated an airmail contract with Sun Fo the son of Sun Yat-sen the
George Washington of China but Sun Fo's reputation was something less
impressive than that of Caesar's wife.
Then too he was at the time
Minister of Railways which Ministry had nothing whatever to do with
mail as that was the business of the Ministry of Communications. The
contract was wonderful but it just happened to be with the wrong out-
The Minister of Communications refused to give the company any
mail or make the subsidy payments called for by the contract. Instead
he set up his own rival airline and bought five Stinson single motor
monoplanes to be managed and flown by Chinese pilots.
As a result
both companies lost money at such an alarming rate that C. M. Keyes
empLoyed Max Polin, & Shanghai business man to work out a consolidation
of the two companies.
The Minister of Communications readily agreed
to this proposal because not only was his company losing money but
under the Chinese management they were also losing airplanes and he
was quite prepared to set up a new company under American operating
managers.
The new company - China National Aviation Corp. - was form-
ed with the Ministry of Communications owning 51% and the Curtiss int-
erests owning the other 49%.. The new company was to have three routes
Shanghai to Peiping, Shanghai to Chungking and Chengtu, Shanghai to
There were
to be seven directors - four representing the
Chinese interests and three the American.
There were to be three
departments - the Business Dept. with a Chinese manager and an American
Assistant - the Finance Department with the same arrangement and an

a Chinese assistant. The
Chinese personnel wanted to get into the Operations Department because
employment was secure there while in the Chinese run divisions employ-
ment usually ended with a change of political leadership - not infrege

ent because the Minister of Communications seldom held office for more
than a few years and each new appointee wanted to have his own team.
The company did not receive any subsidy from the Chinese Government.
Its only revenue came from the carriage of passengers and airmail
which was carried under a unique and most satisfactory arrangement.
If a letter was sent by ordinary mail the sender put on a five cent
stamp and from that revenue the Post Office had to pay for rail or
boat transportation.
If the letter was sent airmail the sender added
to the five cent stamp whatever the airmail postage cost and this entire
surcharge went to the airline. So that the premium for airmail service
went to the company which provided the expedited service while the
Post Office retained the five cents to cover local pickup and delivery.
Every six months the Post Office,
with representatives of the airline
present, counted the number of units of mail per kilo (2.2 Ibs) and
that became the basis of payment by the Post Office to the airline for
the next six months. The unit of mail was 20 grams and the airmail sur-
charge was 25 cents so that if each letter had weighed the limit or
20 grams there would have been 50 units of postage per lilo but of
course many letters weighed much less than the limit and others which
carried two units of postage weighed less than 40 grams. It happened
without exception that each semi-annual test showed that the mail ran
84 letters or units to the kilo so the airline got 21 dollars per kilo
or expressed in U.S. dollars at the average exchange rate about $3.20
per pound - a very good rate.
we had lots of trouble in China with "face" but we put that national
trait to good use by advertising that it your letter was important 1t
was sent by airmail.
The result was that many letters went by air
just because the sender didn't want to lose face.
Pan American bought the American interest in C.N.A.C. in April 1933.
The first meeting of the Board which I attended was called to consider
whether or not the Directors would declare the company insolvent!
Under Chinese Company law if the directors knew or had reason to be-
lieve that their company was insolvent and failed to announce that
fact each of them was personally responsible for the debts of the
company. Actually the company had not been able to pay its bills for
oil and gasoline and owed quite a lot of money to different suppliers
but it was pointed out to the directors that with Pan American spon-
sorship things would get better - but we did not know just how. At
any rate the directors agreed to postpone the announcement and also
agreed to eliminate a zone system which had been in effect for airmail
and follow Pan American's suggestion to have only one zone for all
China so as to popularize and simplify the use of airmail. That was
the turning point and we soon started making modest earnings which
enabled us to pay off our creditors.
Up to that time C.N.A.C. had
been so poor that no Chinese official had tried to get squeeze from
the company or put any of his poor relatives on such an uncertain
payroll.
As we gradually got out of debt and started to pile up
cash balances we realized that a lot of cash would simply open
the
doors to a flood
of demands from Chinese polititians for squeeze and
favors.
So realizing that polititians from F.D.R. down or up are
incapable of reading or understanding a financial statement we started
buying certificates of deposit from Chinese banks (at 8% interest)
and carrying such in our financial statements as "bills receivable"
